fields.questionText:
(a) Define a universal indicator. Mention its one use.
(b) Solution 'A' gives pink colour when a drop of phenolphthalein indicator is added to it. Solution 'B' gives a red colour when a drop of methyl orange is added to it. What type of solutions are 'A' and 'B' and which of these will have higher pH?

fields.answer: (a) A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators that shows different colours at different pH values; it is used to find the approximate pH (strength) of a solution. solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators showing different colours at different pH values; use: to determine the approximate pH / strength of an acid or base.
[1 mark] (b) Phenolphthalein turns pink in a base, so 'A' is basic; methyl orange turns red in an acid, so 'B' is acidic; hence 'A' has the higher pH (> 7).
[1 mark] (c) Na2CO3 (salt of strong base + weak acid) gives pH > 7; NH4Cl (salt of strong acid + weak base) gives pH < 7.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Mixture of indicators; finds pH. (b) A basic, B acidic; A has higher pH. (c) Na2CO3 (pH > 7); NH4Cl (pH < 7).

fields.questionText:
In the chlor-alkali process, electrolysis of brine gives gas 'X' (chlorine) at the anode and gas 'Y' (hydrogen) at the cathode.
(i) Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction that takes place when 'X' and 'Y' react with each other.
(ii) The product so formed turns blue litmus red only when it is wet, not when dry. Why?
fields.answer: (i) H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. (ii) Dry HCl gas does not release H+ ions; only in the presence of water does it ionise (HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−), and these H+ ions turn blue litmus red.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g).
[1 mark] (ii) HCl shows acidic behaviour only in water: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−; dry HCl gives no H+ ions, so only wet HCl turns blue litmus red.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl; (ii) H+ (H3O+) ions form only in the presence of water.

fields.questionText:
pH is measured using a pH meter, which comprises a detecting unit consisting of a pH sensitive glass electrode and an indicating unit which displays the pH reading on a screen.

To measure the pH of a solution, the glass electrode is dipped into the solution and the pH is displayed on the screen of the indicating unit. Before measuring the pH of another solution, the glass electrode is rinsed with distilled water and dried carefully with tissue paper.

(ii) if the second solution being measured is basic in nature

fields.questionText:
A student conducts an experiment with three compounds: methane (CH₄), ethene (C₂H₄) and ethyne (C₂H₂). She burns each in air and also adds each to bromine water.

(i) Write the balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of methane. (1 mark)
(ii) State what is observed when each of the three compounds is passed through bromine water. (1 mark)
(iii) Explain why methane behaves differently from ethene and ethyne with bromine water, and name the type of reaction that occurs (a) on burning and (b) with bromine water. (2 marks)
fields.answer: (i) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. (ii) Methane: no change (bromine water stays orange-brown); ethene and ethyne: bromine water is decolourised. (iii) Methane is saturated (only C–C/C–H single bonds) so it cannot undergo addition; ethene (C=C) and ethyne (C≡C) are unsaturated and add bromine across the multiple bond. Burning = combustion (oxidation); bromine water = addition reaction.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. (ii) Methane: no change (bromine water stays orange-brown); ethene and ethyne: bromine water is decolourised. (iii) Methane is saturated (only C–C/C–H single bonds) so it cannot undergo addition; ethene (C=C) and ethyne (C≡C) are unsaturated and add bromine across the multiple bond. Burning = combustion (oxidation); bromine water = addition reaction.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Complete combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (+ heat and light).
[1 mark] (ii) Methane: no change, bromine water stays orange-brown. Ethene and ethyne: orange-brown colour of bromine water disappears (decolourised).
[1 mark] (iii) Methane is a saturated hydrocarbon (single bonds only), so bromine cannot add to it; ethene (C=C) and ethyne (C≡C) are unsaturated, so bromine adds across the multiple bond.
[1 mark] (iii) Burning in air is combustion, an oxidation reaction; reaction with bromine water is an addition reaction.

fields.questionText:
A student tried to wash a greasy plate using soap in hard water. The soap did not work effectively and a white, curdy precipitate (scum) formed. Later, the student used a detergent in the same water and the plate was cleaned effectively without any precipitate.

(i) Why did the soap fail to clean the plate in hard water? (1 mark)
(ii) What is the white precipitate formed? (1 mark)
(iii) Why does a detergent work well in hard water? Also state one advantage and one disadvantage of detergents compared with soaps. (2 marks)
fields.answer: (i) Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions of hard water react with soap to form an insoluble precipitate, so soap is wasted and little lather forms. (ii) Insoluble calcium/magnesium salt of the fatty acid (e.g. calcium stearate) — scum. (iii) The charged (sulphonate/sulphate) ends of detergents do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; advantage: effective in hard water; disadvantage: many detergents are non-biodegradable.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions which react with soap (RCOONa) to form an insoluble precipitate (RCOO)₂Ca, so the soap is used up and does not form lather or clean.
[1 mark] (ii) The white precipitate (scum) is the insoluble calcium/magnesium salt of the fatty acid, e.g. calcium stearate.
[1 mark] (iii) Detergents are sodium salts of sulphonic acids / ammonium salts; their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions, so they remain effective in hard water.
[1 mark] (iii) Advantage: works well in hard water (no scum). Disadvantage: many detergents are non-biodegradable and cause water pollution.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions form insoluble salts with soap; (ii) calcium/magnesium salt of fatty acid (e.g. calcium stearate) — scum; (iii) charged ends of detergents do not precipitate with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; advantage — works in hard water; disadvantage — non-biodegradable

fields.questionText: Carbon shows two unique properties, catenation and tetravalency. Explain how each of these properties helps carbon form an enormous variety of compounds, and how together they lead to structural diversity among carbon compounds.
fields.answer: Catenation: carbon forms strong C–C bonds and links with other carbon atoms to give long straight chains, branched chains and rings. Tetravalency: carbon (valency 4) bonds with four other atoms — C, H, O, N, S, halogens — giving compounds with different functional groups. Together, the same molecular formula can have different arrangements (structural isomers, e.g. two isomers of butane C4H10), so a huge variety of compounds forms.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Catenation: carbon atoms form strong, stable C–C covalent bonds, so they link into long straight chains, branched chains and closed rings.

[1 mark] Tetravalency: with valency 4, a carbon atom can bond with four other atoms of carbon or of other elements (H, O, N, S, Cl), giving compounds with different functional groups (e.g. –OH, –CHO, –COOH).

[1 mark] Structural diversity: chains/rings plus different attached atoms allow the same molecular formula to have different structures (structural isomers, e.g. n-butane and its branched isomer for C4H10), so millions of carbon compounds exist.
fields.finalAnswer: Catenation gives chains, branches and rings; tetravalency lets carbon bond with four atoms of many elements/functional groups; together they allow different structures (isomers) for the same formula, giving an enormous variety of compounds.

fields.questionText:
Consider the reaction between sodium and chlorine: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

(a) Show, using electron-dot structures, the transfer of electrons in this reaction.
(b) Identify which reactant is oxidised and which is reduced, in terms of loss or gain of electrons.
(c) Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
(d) Explain why this is a redox reaction.
(e) Classify this reaction as combination, decomposition, displacement or double displacement. Justify.
fields.answer: Na is oxidised (reducing agent) and Cl₂ is reduced (oxidising agent); it is a redox reaction and also a combination reaction.
fields.finalAnswer: Na is oxidised (reducing agent) and Cl₂ is reduced (oxidising agent); it is a redox reaction and also a combination reaction.
solutionSteps: (a) Na• → Na⁺ + e⁻ and :Cl: (7 valence electrons) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (8 electrons); Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract to form Na⁺Cl⁻ — one electron passes from each Na atom to each Cl atom.
(b) Na loses an electron (0 → +1), so Na is oxidised; Cl gains an electron (0 → −1), so Cl₂ is reduced.
(c) Reducing agent: Na (it gives electrons and itself gets oxidised). Oxidising agent: Cl₂ (it accepts electrons and itself gets reduced).
(d) Oxidation (loss of electrons by Na) and reduction (gain of electrons by Cl) occur simultaneously in the same reaction, so it is a redox reaction.
(e) Combination reaction: two elements, Na and Cl₂, combine to form a single product, NaCl.

fields.questionText: Two circles with centres O and N touch each other externally at point P, so that O, P and N are collinear. The radius of the circle with centre O is twice that of the circle with centre N. OX is a tangent from O to the circle with centre N, touching it at X, and OX = 18 cm. What is the radius of the circle with centre N?
solutionSteps: Let radius of circle N = r, so radius of circle O = 2r; touching externally, ON = 2r + r = 3r. Radius NX ⊥ tangent OX, so in right ΔOXN: ON² = OX² + NX² ⟹ 9r² = 324 + r² ⟹ 8r² = 324 ⟹ r² = 81/2 ⟹ r = 9/√2 cm → option (c).

fields.questionText:
PQ is a diameter of a circle with centre O. R is a point on the circle at which a tangent is drawn. A line through O parallel to PR meets this tangent at S. Show that SQ is a tangent to the circle.
OR
A circle has centre O. Tangents drawn at points A and C of the circle intersect at B. If OA ⊥ OC, show that quadrilateral OABC is a square.
solutionSteps: [Variant 1] OR ⊥ RS (tangent ⊥ radius). OP = OR ⇒ ∠OPR = ∠ORP. Since OS ∥ PR: ∠ROS = ∠ORP (alternate angles) and ∠QOS = ∠OPR (corresponding angles) ⇒ ∠ROS = ∠QOS.
In △ORS and △OQS: OR = OQ (radii), ∠ROS = ∠QOS, OS common ⇒ △ORS ≅ △OQS (SAS) ⇒ ∠OQS = ∠ORS = 90°.
OQ ⊥ SQ at Q, which lies on the circle ⇒ SQ is a tangent at Q.
[Variant 2] ∠OAB = ∠OCB = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius) and ∠AOC = 90° (given) ⇒ ∠ABC = 360° − 270° = 90°, so OABC is a rectangle.
OA = OC (radii) — adjacent sides of the rectangle are equal (also BA = BC, tangents from B) ⇒ OABC is a square.
fields.strategyHint: Use tangent ⊥ radius and congruence (SAS) for Variant 1; for Variant 2 show all angles 90° and adjacent sides equal.

fields.questionText:
A circular fountain in a park has centre O and radius 5 m. A lamp post stands at point P, 13 m from O. Two straight paths PA and PB run from the lamp post and just touch the fountain's boundary at A and B.
(i) Find the length of path PA. [1]
(ii) What is the measure of ∠OAP? Give a reason. [1]
(iii) Find the area of the quadrilateral OAPB enclosed by the two paths and the radii OA and OB. [2]
fields.answer: (i) PA = 12 m (ii) ∠OAP = 90°, since the tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through it (iii) 60 m²
fields.explanation: PA is a tangent, so OA ⊥ PA and PA = √(OP² − OA²) = √(169 − 25) = 12 m. PA = PB (tangents from an external point), so △OAP ≅ △OBP and area OAPB = 2 × ½ × 5 × 12 = 60 m².
solutionSteps: (ii) ∠OAP = 90°, because the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. [1]
(iii) PA = PB = 12 m and OA = OB, so △OAP ≅ △OBP; area △OAP = ½ × OA × PA = ½ × 5 × 12 = 30 m². [1]
Area of OAPB = 2 × 30 = 60 m². [1]

fields.questionText: A circle with centre O has radius 6 cm. From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn to the circle such that the tangents are perpendicular to each other. Find OP and the length of each tangent, and verify your answer.
solutionSteps: Since ∠APB = 90° and OP bisects ∠APB, ∠OPA = 45°; also OA ⊥ PA (radius ⊥ tangent), so triangle OAP is right-angled at A.
sin 45° = OA/OP ⇒ OP = 6/sin 45° = 6√2 cm.
Tangent length PA = OP × cos 45° = 6√2 × (1/√2) = 6 cm (so PB = 6 cm too).
Verification: OA² + PA² = 36 + 36 = 72 = (6√2)² = OP². ✓
fields.finalAnswer: OP = 6√2 cm; each tangent length = 6 cm.

fields.questionText:
Attempt either (a) or (b).
(a) "The timing and the amount of hormone secreted by a gland are regulated in the human body." Justify this statement with the help of an example.
OR
(b) Electrical impulse is an excellent means to transmit information in the animal body, but there are some limitations to the use of electrical impulses. State any two limitations.
fields.answer: (a) The timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by a feedback mechanism. Example: when blood sugar level rises, it is detected by cells of the pancreas, which secrete more insulin; as blood sugar falls, insulin secretion is reduced. (Any other suitable example.) OR (b) (1) Electrical impulses reach only those cells that are connected by nervous tissue, not each and every cell of the body. (2) Once a cell generates and transmits an impulse, it takes time to reset its mechanism before it can generate a new impulse, so cells cannot continually create and transmit impulses.
solutionSteps: (a) The timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by a feedback mechanism.
(a) Example: when blood sugar level rises, the pancreas cells detect it and secrete more insulin; as blood sugar falls, insulin secretion is reduced. (Any other suitable example.)
OR (b) Limitation 1: Electrical impulses reach only those cells that are connected by nervous tissue, not each and every cell in the body.
(b) Limitation 2: After generating and transmitting an impulse, a cell takes time to reset its mechanism before it can transmit a new one, so transmission is not continuous.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Feedback mechanism — e.g. rise in blood sugar → more insulin from pancreas; fall → less insulin. OR (b) Impulses reach only cells connected by nervous tissue; cells need time to reset before a new impulse, so transmission is not continuous.

fields.questionText:
(a) (i) List three points of difference between nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals.
(ii) How are auxins related with the bending of plant shoot towards unidirectional light? Explain.
OR
(b) (i) Name the disorder which a person is likely to suffer from due to the following:
(I) Over-secretion of growth hormone
(II) Deficiency of oestrogen in females
(III) Less secretion of thyroxine
Also name the gland that secretes each of the hormones mentioned above.
(ii) How is the timing and amount of hormone released regulated? Explain with the help of an example.
fields.answer: (a)(i) Nervous control: messages as electrical impulses, carried through neurons, rapid and short-lived responses. Hormonal control: messages as chemicals (hormones), carried through blood, slow and long-lasting responses. (ii) In unidirectional light, auxin diffuses to the shaded side of the shoot; the cells there grow longer, so the shoot bends towards light. OR (b)(i) (I) Gigantism – pituitary; (II) delayed/absence of puberty changes – ovary; (III) goitre – thyroid. (ii) By feedback mechanisms, e.g. when blood sugar rises, more insulin is secreted; as it falls, insulin secretion is reduced.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a)(i) Nervous: messages sent as electrical impulses; Hormonal: messages carried as chemicals (hormones).
[1 mark] Nervous: carried through neurons; Hormonal: carried through blood.
[1 mark] Nervous: rapid, short-lived responses; Hormonal: slow, long-lasting responses.
[1 mark] (a)(ii) When the growing shoot is exposed to unidirectional light, auxin diffuses towards the shaded side of the shoot.
[1 mark] The higher auxin concentration makes cells on the shaded side grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light.
OR (b)(i) (I) Gigantism – pituitary gland; (II) delayed puberty / failure of secondary sexual characters – ovary; (III) goitre – thyroid gland. [½ mark each for disorder and gland = 3 marks]

(b)(ii) Timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by feedback mechanisms [1 mark]. Example: when blood sugar level rises, the pancreas secretes more insulin; as the level falls, insulin secretion is reduced [1 mark].
fields.finalAnswer: (a)(i) Nervous – electrical impulses, via neurons, rapid & short-lived; hormonal – chemicals, via blood, slow & long-lasting. (ii) Auxin moves to the shaded side, cells there elongate, shoot bends to light. OR (b)(i) Gigantism–pituitary; delayed puberty–ovary; goitre–thyroid. (ii) Feedback mechanism, e.g. insulin and blood sugar.

fields.questionText: Three identical bulbs B₁, B₂ and B₃ are connected in parallel across a 4.5 V battery. (i) What happens to the glow of the other two bulbs when the bulb B₁ gets fused? (ii) What happens to the readings of A₁, A₂, A₃ and A when the bulb B₂ gets fused? (iii) How much power is dissipated in the circuit when all the three bulbs glow together?
fields.answer: The three identical bulbs are in parallel across the 4.5 V battery, so with a total current of 3 A each bulb carries 1 A. [1 mark] (i) If B₁ is fused, only the B₁ branch is broken. The other two branches still get full voltage and continue to glow as before (no change in brightness).
[1 mark] (ii) If B₂ fuses: A₂ → 0; A₁ and A₃ remain 1 A each; the main ammeter A drops from 3 A to 1 + 1 = 2 A.
[1 mark] (iii) Power dissipated when all three bulbs glow = V × I_total, with V = 4.5 V and I_total = 3 A.

fields.answer: The two 8 Ω resistors are in parallel and this combination is in series with the 4 Ω resistor and the 8 V battery. (a) R_p = (8 × 8)/(8 + 8) = 4 Ω. (b) Total resistance = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω, so I = 8 V / 8 Ω = 1 A through the 4 Ω resistor. (c) V across 4 Ω = 1 × 4 = 4 V. (d) P in 4 Ω = I²R = 1² × 4 = 4 W. (e) Both ammeters are in the same series line, so they read the same (1 A) — difference 0.
solutionSteps: [0.5 mark] The two 8 Ω resistors are in parallel; this block is in series with the 4 Ω resistor and the 8 V battery.
[1 mark] (a) Effective resistance of the two 8 Ω resistors in parallel: R_p = (8 × 8)/(8 + 8) = 64/16 = 4 Ω.
[1.5 marks] (b) Total resistance R = R_p + 4 = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω; current I = V/R = 8 V / 8 Ω = 1 A, and being in series the 4 Ω resistor carries this 1 A.
[0.5 mark] (c) Potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor: V₄ = IR = 1 × 4 = 4 V.
[0.5 mark] (d) Power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor: P₄ = I²R = 1² × 4 = 4 W.
[1 mark] (e) Both ammeters A₁ and A₂ are in the same series line and carry the same current (1 A), so the difference in their readings is 0.

fields.answer: (i) Live wire – red; neutral wire – black; earth wire – green. (ii) 220 V. (iii) (I) Earthing provides a low-resistance conducting path to the earth for any current leaking to the metallic body of an appliance, keeping the body at earth potential and protecting the user from electric shock. (II) A fuse is a safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when an unduly high current flows (overloading/short-circuit), preventing damage to appliances and the circuit.

fields.questionText: In some families, either rural or urban, females are tortured for giving birth to a female child. They do not seem to understand the scientific reason behind the birth of a boy or a girl. In fact the mother is not responsible for the sex of the child and it has been genetically proved that the sex of a newborn is determined by what the child inherits from the father. (a) State the basis on which the sex of a newborn baby is determined in humans. (b) Why is the pair of sex chromosomes called a mismatched pair in males? (c) How is the original number of chromosomes present in the parents restored in the progeny? OR (c) Explain by giving two examples of the organisms in which the sex is not genetically determined.
fields.answer: (a) Sex is determined by the sex chromosome the child inherits from the father: X from father + X from mother → girl (XX); Y from father + X from mother → boy (XY). (b) In males the pair is mismatched because X is normal-sized while Y is short. (c) Gametes have half the number of chromosomes; fusion of male and female gametes at fertilisation restores the original number. OR (c) Some reptiles — incubation temperature of fertilised eggs determines sex; snails — individuals can change sex during their lifetime.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Sex is determined by the sex chromosome the child inherits from the father: X from father + X from mother → girl (XX); Y from father + X from mother → boy (XY). (b) In males the pair is mismatched because X is normal-sized while Y is short. (c) Gametes have half the number of chromosomes; fusion of male and female gametes at fertilisation restores the original number. OR (c) Some reptiles — incubation temperature of fertilised eggs determines sex; snails — individuals can change sex during their lifetime.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) The sex chromosome inherited from the father: if a sperm carrying X fuses with the ovum (always X), a girl (XX) is born; if a sperm carrying Y fuses with the ovum, a boy (XY) is born.
[1 mark] (b) Because one of them is a normal-sized X chromosome while the other is a short Y chromosome.

[1 mark] (c) During formation of germ cells (gametes) the chromosome number is reduced to half. OR (c) Example 1: in some reptiles, the temperature at which the fertilised eggs are kept determines whether the young will be male or female.

[1 mark] When two germ cells from two individuals fuse during fertilisation, the original number of chromosomes is restored in the progeny. OR Example 2: in snails, individuals can change sex during their lifetime.

fields.answer: (a) Mendel, working on the garden pea (Pisum sativum), found that traits are controlled by 'factors' (now called genes) present in pairs, one inherited from each parent. (b) Of a pair of contrasting traits, one is dominant and expresses itself, while the other is recessive and is masked in the hybrid (F1) — Law of Dominance. (c) The two factors of a pair separate (segregate) during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one factor; they recombine at fertilisation — Law of Segregation (and with two traits, they assort independently — Law of Independent Assortment).
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Traits are controlled by factors (genes) that occur in pairs; one factor of each pair is inherited from each parent.
[1 mark] Dominance: of two contrasting factors, one (dominant) is expressed in the F1 and the other (recessive) is masked.
[1 mark] Segregation: the paired factors separate during gamete formation so each gamete gets only one, and they recombine at fertilisation; for two traits they assort independently.

fields.questionText:
A couple has three children: two boys and one girl. They want to know the probability of their next child being a boy. The woman says, 'Since we have had two boys, the next child is more likely to be a girl to balance the ratio.' The man says, 'Each child has an equal 50% chance of being a boy or a girl, regardless of previous children.'

(i) Who is correct — the man or the woman? (1)
(ii) What is the probability that their next child will be a boy? (1)
(iii) With the help of a cross between the sex chromosomes of the parents, explain why each child has an equal chance of being a boy or a girl. (2)
solutionSteps: (i) [1 mark] The man is correct: the sex of each child is decided independently at fertilisation; previous children do not affect the next one.
(ii) [1 mark] Probability of a boy = 1/2 = 50%.
(iii) [1 mark] Cross: mother (XX) × father (XY). The mother's eggs all carry X; the father produces two kinds of sperm in equal numbers — half with X, half with Y.
(iii) [1 mark] X-sperm + X-egg → XX (girl); Y-sperm + X-egg → XY (boy). Offspring XX : XY = 1 : 1, so every child has a 50% chance of being a boy, independent of earlier children.

fields.questionText: Explain Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment using a dihybrid cross between a pea plant with round, yellow seeds (RRYY) and one with wrinkled, green seeds (rryy). Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y). Give the F₁ result, the gametes formed by F₁, the F₂ phenotypes with their ratio, and explain how this ratio shows independent assortment.
fields.answer: F₁ all RrYy (round, yellow); F₁ gametes RY, Ry, rY, ry; F₂ = 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) show the two traits are inherited independently.
fields.finalAnswer: F₂ ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green) — new combinations prove independent assortment.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Law: when two pairs of traits are crossed, the factors of each pair are inherited independently of the other pair during gamete formation.
[1 mark] Parents RRYY (round, yellow) × rryy (wrinkled, green) → F₁ all RrYy (round, yellow).
[1 mark] F₁ selfed (RrYy × RrYy): each F₁ plant forms four kinds of gametes RY, Ry, rY, ry in equal numbers; a 4 × 4 Punnett square gives 16 combinations.
[1 mark] F₂ phenotypes: 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.

[1 mark] Besides the parental types, new combinations (round green and wrinkled yellow) appear; each trait still separately shows 3 : 1 (12 round : 4 wrinkled; 12 yellow : 4 green), proving the two traits assort independently.

fields.questionText: Mention the total number of chromosomes, along with the sex chromosomes, in human beings. Explain how, in a sexually reproducing organism, the chromosome number of the parents and their offspring remains the same.
fields.answer: Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes — XX in females and XY in males. Germ cells (gametes) are formed in specialised reproductive organs and carry only half the number of chromosomes (and half the DNA) of body cells. When a male and a female gamete fuse at fertilisation, the zygote gets the full (original) chromosome number back, so offspring have the same chromosome number as the parents.
solutionSteps: Humans have 46 chromosomes, i.e. 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).
Gametes are formed in specialised reproductive organs and contain only half the number of chromosomes and half the DNA of a body cell (23 in humans).
At fertilisation a male and a female gamete fuse (23 + 23 = 46), restoring the original chromosome number in the zygote; hence parents and offspring have the same chromosome number.
fields.finalAnswer: 46 chromosomes (22 pairs autosomes + XX/XY); gametes are haploid and fertilisation restores the full number, keeping it constant across generations.

fields.answer: (a) Male part: stamen (anther + filament); female part: pistil/carpel (stigma + style + ovary). (b) Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma; self-pollination is transfer within the same flower (or another flower of the same plant), cross-pollination is transfer to the stigma of a flower on a different plant. (c) After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo; the ovule develops into the seed and the ovary into the fruit, while petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma wither. (d) Humans are unisexual with separate male and female individuals, have internal fertilisation in the oviduct and the embryo develops in the uterus nourished through the placenta; flowering plants are often bisexual, need pollination before fertilisation, and the embryo develops inside the seed.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Male reproductive part: stamen (anther + filament); female reproductive part: pistil/carpel (stigma + style + ovary).

[1 mark] (b) Pollination: transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination – pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower (or another flower of the same plant); cross-pollination – pollen reaches the stigma of a flower on a different plant.

[1 mark] (c) After fertilisation the zygote divides to form the embryo; the ovule develops into the seed and the ovary ripens into the fruit; petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma wither and fall off.

[1 mark] (d) Humans: separate sexes, internal fertilisation in the oviduct, embryo develops in the uterus and is nourished through the placenta. Flowering plants: flowers are often bisexual, pollination is needed to bring pollen to the stigma, and the embryo develops and is stored inside the seed.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Stamen; pistil. (b) Pollen transfer anther→stigma; self = same flower/plant, cross = different plant. (c) Ovule→seed, ovary→fruit. (d) Humans: separate sexes, internal fertilisation, placenta; plants: often bisexual, pollination needed, embryo in seed.

fields.questionText:
All the reproductive methods of living organisms are broadly categorized into two types: 1. Asexual reproduction, and 2. Sexual reproduction. Asexual reproduction involves the participation of a single parent without the formation of gametes, fertilisation and transfer of genetic material. This method is a common means of rapidly increasing offspring under favourable conditions.
(a) Name the type of fission that occurs in Leishmania and Plasmodium. (1)
(b) Write one advantage of sexual mode of reproduction over asexual reproduction. (1)
(c) Give reasons why: (i) Colonies of yeast fail to multiply in water but multiply in sugar solution. (ii) Rhizopus individuals do not grow on a dry slice of bread. (2)
OR
(c) Name the filamentous structures a student could identify when he collected water from a pond that appeared dark green. How do these organisms multiply? Explain. (2)
fields.answer: (a) Leishmania – binary fission; Plasmodium – multiple fission. (b) Sexual reproduction produces variations that help the species survive. (c)(i) Sugar solution provides nutrients for growth and multiplication, water does not. (ii) Rhizopus needs moisture to grow. OR (c) Spirogyra; it multiplies by fragmentation – the mature filament breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new individual.
solutionSteps: [½ + ½ mark] (a) Leishmania – binary fission; Plasmodium – multiple fission.
[1 mark] (b) Sexual reproduction leads to more variations, which are useful for ensuring the survival of a species.
[1 mark] (c)(i) Sugar solution provides nutrients (food) for growth and multiplication of yeast, whereas water does not.
[1 mark] (c)(ii) Moisture is required for the growth of Rhizopus; a dry slice of bread lacks it.

OR (c) [½ mark] The filaments are Spirogyra. [½ mark] They multiply by fragmentation. [1 mark] On maturing, the filament simply breaks up into smaller pieces and each piece grows into a new individual.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Leishmania – binary fission; Plasmodium – multiple fission. (b) Variation aids survival of the species. (c)(i) Sugar gives nutrients, water does not; (ii) Rhizopus needs moisture. OR (c) Spirogyra – fragmentation; each broken piece grows into a new individual.

fields.questionText:
Given below are certain situations. Analyse and describe its possible impact on a person:
(a) Testes of a male boy are not able to descend into scrotum during his embryonic development.
(b) Vas deferens of a man is plugged.
(c) Prostate and seminal vesicles are not functional.
(d) Egg is not fertilised in a human female.
(e) Placenta does not attach to the uterus optimally.
fields.answer: (a) Sperm formation is impaired as testes need a lower-than-body temperature. (b) Sperms cannot be transferred – infertility. (c) Sperms lack nourishment and fluid medium for transport. (d) Egg survives about a day; uterine lining breaks down – menstruation. (e) Embryo gets inadequate nutrition and oxygen – growth affected.
solutionSteps: (a) Sperm formation will be adversely affected because spermatogenesis requires a temperature lower than core body temperature (the scrotum keeps testes ~2 °C cooler). Undescended testes → reduced or absent sperm production.
(b) Vas deferens is the passage for sperm transfer from testis to urethra. If plugged, sperms cannot be transferred further — leading to infertility despite normal sperm production.
(c) Prostate gland and seminal vesicles produce secretions that nourish sperm and form the medium (semen) for sperm transport. If non-functional, sperms lack nourishment and proper transport medium.

(d) If the egg is not fertilised, it lives for about one day. Then the thickened lining of the uterus breaks, leading to discharge of blood and mucus along with the unfertilised egg — this is called menstruation.
(e) Placenta provides nutrition and oxygen to the growing embryo. Sub-optimal attachment will impair nutrition and oxygen supply, affecting embryo growth and possibly causing serious complications.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Sperm formation impaired; (b) sperm transfer blocked – infertility; (c) sperms lack nourishment/transport medium; (d) menstruation follows; (e) embryo's nutrition and oxygen supply impaired.

fields.answer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones) with little or no variation, so the population is less adaptable and may be wiped out by a change in the environment or a disease. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents, producing variation among offspring; some variants may survive a changed environment, so the species is more adaptable and its survival is ensured.
solutionSteps: Asexual reproduction: one parent, no fusion of gametes, so offspring are clones (genetically identical) with little or no variation (only minor variation from DNA copying errors).
Sexual reproduction: two parents; fusion of gametes combines DNA from both, so offspring show considerable variation.

Adaptability: with no variation, all asexually produced individuals may be destroyed by the same environmental change or disease; variation from sexual reproduction means some individuals may survive the change, ensuring survival of the species.
fields.finalAnswer: Asexual: one parent, clones, little variation – less adaptable. Sexual: two parents, gamete fusion, variation – some offspring survive environmental change, so the species is more adaptable.

fields.questionText:
A person allowed a narrow beam of white light from the sun to enter a dark room through a small aperture and placed a glass prism in its path in such a manner that the beam falls on the face AB of the prism as shown in the figure. A screen S is placed on the other side of the prism, facing AC. On turning the prism slowly, a beautiful band of colours is obtained on the screen. It is the spectrum of sunlight.
(a) Name the phenomenon due to which a prism splits the incident white light into a band of colours. (1)
(b) State the reason for getting a band of seven colours in the above case. (1)
(c) (i) Explain with the help of a labelled ray diagram an experimental arrangement to show the recombination of the spectrum of white light. (2)
OR
(c) (ii) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the formation of a rainbow. (2)
fields.answer: (a) Dispersion of light. (b) Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism. (c)(i) Two identical prisms are placed in inverted position with respect to each other; when the spectrum produced by prism A passes through prism B, a beam of white light emerges from prism B. OR (c)(ii) Labelled diagram: sunlight refracted and dispersed on entering a raindrop, internally reflected at the back, refracted again on leaving, red and violet emerging separately.
solutionSteps: (a) Dispersion of light.
(b) Different colours of white light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism, so they separate into seven colours.
(c)(i) Diagram: two identical prisms A and B, with B placed inverted with respect to A; white light enters A, is dispersed into a spectrum which then falls on B.
(c)(i) The spectrum produced by prism A, on passing through prism B, recombines and a beam of white light emerges from the other side of prism B.
OR (c)(ii) Diagram: a raindrop with sunlight refracted and dispersed on entering, internally reflected at the back surface, and refracted again on emerging, with red and violet rays labelled.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) Dispersion. (b) Different colours bend through different angles in the prism. (c)(i) Two identical prisms, the second inverted, recombine the spectrum into white light. OR (c)(ii) Rainbow: refraction + dispersion, internal reflection, refraction in a raindrop.

fields.questionText:
Case Study: Rajesh, a 45-year-old man, visits an eye clinic complaining that he can see distant objects clearly but has difficulty reading newspapers. His daughter, who is 12 years old, complains that she cannot see the board at school clearly but can read books comfortably. Both require different types of lenses for correction.

(i) What is the vision defect of Rajesh, and what type of lens would he need? (1)
(ii) Identify the vision defect of Rajesh's daughter and suggest an appropriate lens type. (1)
(iii) Explain the role of the ciliary muscles in accommodation and why accommodation fails in Rajesh's case. (2)
fields.answer: (i) Rajesh has presbyopia; he needs a convex lens. (ii) The daughter has myopia; she needs a concave lens. (iii) Ciliary muscles change the curvature (and focal length) of the eye lens for accommodation. In presbyopia, ageing weakens the ciliary muscles and reduces the flexibility of the eye lens, so the lens cannot become thick enough for near vision.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) He sees far objects clearly but not near ones at age 45 → presbyopia; corrected with a convex lens.
[1 mark] (ii) She cannot see distant objects but reads comfortably → myopia; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.
[1 mark] (iii) Ciliary muscles contract or relax to change the curvature and focal length of the eye lens; for near objects they contract, making the lens thicker (more convex).
[1 mark] (iii) In presbyopia, ageing gradually weakens the ciliary muscles and reduces the flexibility of the eye lens, so the near point recedes and near objects cannot be focused.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) Presbyopia, convex lens. (ii) Myopia, concave lens. (iii) Ciliary muscles change lens curvature/focal length; in presbyopia weakened muscles and a less flexible lens prevent accommodation for near vision.

fields.questionText: We need to water the soil in plants on a regular basis. But it ultimately reaches the leaves of the plant. Explain how this takes place.
fields.answer: Water absorbed by the roots moves up through the continuous xylem vessels of root, stem and leaves. Loss of water vapour through stomata of leaves (transpiration) creates a suction force, the transpiration pull, which pulls the water column up from the roots to the leaves.
fields.finalAnswer: Water rises through xylem from roots to leaves, pulled up by the transpiration pull created by loss of water vapour through the stomata.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Roots absorb water from the soil; it moves up through the interconnected xylem vessels of root, stem and leaves.
[1 mark] Evaporation of water through stomata of leaves (transpiration) creates a suction force (transpiration pull) that pulls the water column up to the leaves.

fields.questionText: What is the composition of urine? Are glucose and proteins normally present in urine? Why? How is the volume of urine regulated?
fields.answer: Urine contains mainly water, urea, uric acid and various salts. Glucose and proteins are normally absent: glucose is reabsorbed in the tubules of the nephron, and proteins are too large to be filtered from the blood in the glomerulus of a healthy kidney. The volume of urine depends on (a) the amount of excess water in the body and (b) the amount of dissolved wastes to be excreted.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Composition: mainly water, urea, uric acid and salts.
[1 mark] Glucose and proteins are normally absent: glucose is selectively reabsorbed in the nephron tubule; proteins (large molecules) are not filtered in the glomerulus of a healthy kidney.
[1 mark] Volume of urine is regulated by the amount of excess water in the body and the amount of dissolved wastes to be excreted (by varying reabsorption of water in the tubule).

fields.questionText: Explain how the processes of photosynthesis and respiration together sustain life on Earth.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Photosynthesis: green plants use light energy to make food (glucose/starch) from carbon dioxide and water and release oxygen; this food is the energy source for all food chains (consumers eat plants).
[1 mark] Respiration: living organisms break down food to release energy (ATP) needed for growth, movement, maintaining body temperature and other life processes.
[1 mark] Link: respiration uses the oxygen released by photosynthesis and releases carbon dioxide and water, which are the raw materials of photosynthesis, so the two processes keep each other going.

solutionSteps: [1 mark] Diagram: neat vertical section of the heart labelling the four chambers (right/left atrium, right/left ventricle), septum, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta and valves.
[1 mark] Structure: a muscular four-chambered organ — two upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-walled ventricles; the septum keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

[1 mark] Vessels: right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body by the vena cava, right ventricle pumps it to the lungs by the pulmonary artery; left atrium receives oxygenated blood by the pulmonary vein, left ventricle pumps it to the body through the aorta.
[1 mark] Valves between atria and ventricles and at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery allow blood to flow in one direction only and prevent backflow when chambers contract.
[1 mark] The left ventricle wall is thicker because it pumps blood at high pressure to the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs.

fields.questionText: How is nutrition in a fungus different from that in a tapeworm?
fields.answer: A fungus usually shows saprophytic nutrition: it secretes digestive enzymes onto dead and decaying matter, digests it outside its body and absorbs the products (some fungi are parasitic). A tapeworm is a parasite: it lives in the intestine of its host and absorbs the host's already-digested food through its body surface.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Fungus: saprophytic (or parasitic) nutrition — breaks down food outside the body using enzymes and absorbs it.
[1 mark] Tapeworm: only parasitic nutrition — absorbs digested food from the host's intestine through its body surface.

fields.questionText: (a) How are oxygen and carbon dioxide exchanged between blood and tissues? How are these gases transported in human beings? (b) What is haemoglobin?
fields.answer: (a) Exchange between blood and tissues occurs by diffusion along concentration gradients. Oxygen is carried from the lungs as oxyhaemoglobin; in the tissues it dissociates and diffuses into the cells, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the cells into the blood. Carbon dioxide is transported mostly dissolved in the plasma to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli. (b) Haemoglobin is the red, iron-containing respiratory pigment in red blood cells that has a high affinity for oxygen.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Exchange in tissues is by diffusion: oxygen diffuses from blood into cells; carbon dioxide diffuses from cells into blood.
[1 mark] Transport: oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin; carbon dioxide is carried mostly dissolved in plasma to the lungs.
[1 mark] (b) Haemoglobin is the respiratory pigment (red, iron-containing protein) in red blood cells with high affinity for oxygen.

fields.questionText: How are oxygen and carbon dioxide transported in human beings? Explain clearly how air is inhaled and exhaled during breathing in humans.
fields.answer: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into blood and is carried by haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin to the tissues, where it diffuses into cells; carbon dioxide diffuses from tissues into blood and is carried mostly dissolved in plasma to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out. Inhalation: diaphragm and rib muscles contract, the chest cavity enlarges, pressure falls and air rushes in. Exhalation: these muscles relax, the chest cavity becomes smaller and air is pushed out.

fields.questionText: The absolute refractive indices of some media are: Air 1.0003, Ice 1.31, Water 1.33, Alcohol 1.36, Kerosene 1.44, Turpentine oil 1.47, Crown glass 1.52, Rock salt 1.54, Carbon disulphide 1.63, Dense flint glass 1.65, Ruby 1.71, Sapphire 1.77, Diamond 2.42. From these values, find the medium having the highest optical density and the medium having the lowest optical density.
solutionSteps: [0.5 mark] Optical density is indicated by the refractive index - higher n means optically denser.
[0.5 mark] Compare the given absolute refractive indices for the highest and lowest values.

(B) (i) Draw a diagram showing the magnetic field lines in and around a current carrying solenoid. Write any two salient features of these lines. (ii) What is an electromagnet and how is it made?
fields.subtopic: Magnetic Field Lines, Right-Hand Thumb Rule & Solenoid
fields.answer:
(A) (i) Diagram: closed field lines leaving the N pole and entering the S pole of the bar magnet. Any two: field lines emerge from N and merge at S outside, running S to N inside (closed curves); closeness of lines shows field strength; no two field lines cross. (ii) Hold the current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field lines. (iii) The magnetic field decreases as the circles get larger (farther from the wire).
OR (B) (i) Diagram of solenoid field lines; features: pattern similar to a bar magnet; inside, the lines are parallel straight lines (uniform field). (ii) An electromagnet is a piece of magnetic material (soft iron) that behaves as a magnet only while current flows through the coil around it; it is made by winding insulated copper wire as a coil around a soft-iron core and passing current through it.
solutionSteps: (A)(i) Diagram: magnetic field lines around a bar magnet as closed curves, leaving the N pole and entering the S pole, with arrows marked.

(A)(i) Any two characteristics: outside the magnet the field lines go from N pole to S pole and inside from S to N, so they are closed curves; the closeness of the lines shows the relative strength of the field; no two field lines ever cross each other.

(A)(ii) Right-hand thumb rule: imagine holding a current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand so that the thumb points in the direction of current; then the fingers wrapped around the conductor show the direction of the magnetic field lines.
(A)(iii) As the concentric circles become larger (farther from the wire), the magnetic field on them decreases; the field is inversely proportional to distance from the wire.

OR (B)(i) Diagram: field lines of a current-carrying solenoid, parallel inside and spreading out at the ends like a bar magnet, with direction marked. Any two features: the pattern is similar to that of a bar magnet (one end N, other end S); inside the solenoid the lines are parallel straight lines, showing a uniform field.

(B)(ii) An electromagnet is a magnetic material (soft iron) that behaves like a magnet only while an electric current passes through the coil around it. It is made by winding a coil of insulated copper wire around a soft-iron core (or placing a soft-iron core inside a solenoid) and passing current through the coil.
fields.finalAnswer: (A) Field lines are closed curves N→S outside, do not cross, closeness = strength; right-hand thumb rule as stated; field decreases on larger circles. OR (B) Solenoid field like a bar magnet, uniform parallel lines inside; electromagnet = soft-iron core in a current-carrying coil.

fields.questionText:
(a) (i) A straight cylindrical conductor is suspended with its axis perpendicular to the magnetic field of a horse-shoe magnet. The conductor gets displaced towards left when a current is passed through it. What will happen to the displacement of the conductor if the (1) current through it is increased? (2) horse-shoe magnet is replaced by another stronger horse-shoe magnet? (3) direction of current through it is reversed? (ii) Name and state the rule for determining the direction of force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
OR
(b) Draw the pattern of the magnetic field produced around a vertical current carrying straight conductor passing through a horizontal cardboard. Mark the direction of current and the magnetic field lines. Name and state the rule which is used to determine the direction of magnetic field associated with a current carrying conductor.
fields.answer:
(a)(i) (1) Displacement increases. (2) Displacement increases. (3) Displacement reverses (conductor moves to the right). (ii) Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points along the magnetic field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of force (motion) on the conductor.
OR (b) Concentric circles centred on the wire on the cardboard, direction given by the right-hand thumb rule: holding the conductor in the right hand with the thumb along the current, the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines.
solutionSteps: (a)(i) (1) Increased current → larger force → displacement increases. (2) Stronger magnet → larger force → displacement increases. (3) Current reversed → force reverses → conductor is displaced towards the right.

(a)(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of current, the thumb points in the direction of force (motion) on the conductor.

OR (b) Diagram: concentric circular field lines on the cardboard centred on the wire, with the current direction (e.g. upward) marked on the wire and arrows on the circles (anticlockwise seen from above for upward current).

(b) Right-hand thumb rule: imagine holding the current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of current; the fingers wrapped around it give the direction of the magnetic field lines.
fields.finalAnswer: (a)(i) increases; increases; reverses (moves right). (ii) Fleming's left-hand rule (as stated). OR (b) Concentric circles around the wire; right-hand thumb rule (as stated).

fields.answer: (a) The arrangement of metals in decreasing order of their reactivity is called the reactivity (activity) series. A metal higher in the series is more reactive and can displace a metal lower in the series from its salt solution, so the series predicts the relative activity of metals. (b) Metals in the middle (e.g. Zn, Fe) are first converted to oxides (roasting/calcination) and then reduced with carbon, e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO. Metals at the top (e.g. Na) are obtained by electrolytic reduction of their molten chlorides, e.g. molten NaCl: at cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; at anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) The reactivity series lists metals in decreasing order of reactivity; a metal placed higher can displace a metal placed lower from its salt solution, so the series predicts their relative activity.
[1 mark] (b) Middle of the series: oxide is reduced with carbon (sulphide/carbonate ores are first roasted/calcined to oxide), e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO.
[1 mark] (b) Top of the series: electrolytic reduction of the molten chloride, e.g. molten NaCl — cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
fields.finalAnswer: Reactivity series = metals in decreasing order of reactivity (higher displaces lower). Middle metals: reduction of oxide with carbon (ZnO + C → Zn + CO). Top metals: electrolytic reduction of molten chloride (NaCl → Na at cathode).

fields.question:
Rohan lives in a coastal town and notices that his iron bicycle rusts much faster than his cousin's bicycle in a dry inland town.
(i) Name the two substances that must be present for iron to rust. [1]
(ii) Why does Rohan's bicycle rust faster in the coastal town? [1]
(iii) Suggest two methods to prevent rusting of the bicycle and briefly explain why each method works. [2]
fields.answer: (i) Oxygen (air) and water (moisture). (ii) Coastal air is very humid and carries salt, so more moisture is present and rusting is faster. (iii) Painting/oiling/greasing forms a barrier that keeps air and moisture away from iron; galvanising coats iron with zinc, which is more reactive and corrodes first, protecting iron even if the coating is scratched.
fields.explanation: Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and moisture. Humid, salty coastal air speeds it up. Paint or grease is a physical barrier; zinc in galvanising also gives sacrificial protection because it is more reactive than iron.
solutionSteps: (i) Iron rusts only when both oxygen (air) and water (moisture) are present. [1]
(ii) Coastal air is humid and salty, so more moisture is in contact with iron and rusting is faster. [1]
(iii) Method 1: Painting / applying oil or grease — forms a layer that prevents air and moisture from reaching the iron. [1]
(iii) Method 2: Galvanising — coating with zinc; zinc is more reactive than iron and gets oxidised first, so iron is protected even if the coating is scratched. [1]
fields.finalAnswer: (i) Oxygen and moisture; (ii) humid, salty coastal air; (iii) painting/oiling (barrier) and galvanising (zinc corrodes in preference to iron).

fields.questionText:
A car manufacturer uses three different methods to prevent corrosion of car parts:
Method 1: Painting with a thick protective coating
Method 2: Galvanisation with a zinc layer
Method 3: Using stainless steel (an alloy of iron with chromium and nickel)

(i) How does painting prevent corrosion of the car parts? [1]
(ii) How does galvanisation protect the iron even if the zinc layer gets scratched? [1]
(iii) Why does stainless steel not rust easily, and which of the three methods gives the most effective long-term protection? Justify your answer. [2]
fields.answer: (i) Paint forms a physical barrier that keeps oxygen and moisture away from iron. (ii) Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it gets oxidised first and protects the iron (sacrificial protection). (iii) Alloying iron with chromium and nickel changes its properties so stainless steel does not rust (chromium forms a thin protective oxide layer); Method 3 is most effective long-term because the protection is throughout the metal and does not wear off, whereas paint and zinc coatings can get damaged or wear away.
solutionSteps: (i) Painting creates a physical barrier preventing oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron. [1 mark]
(ii) Zinc is more reactive than iron, gets oxidised in preference to iron and sacrifices itself, so exposed iron is still protected. [1 mark]
(iii) Stainless steel is an alloy; chromium forms a thin, self-repairing oxide layer, so it resists rusting throughout the metal. [1 mark]
(iii) Method 3 is most effective long-term: its protection is not a surface coating that can wear off, unlike paint (Method 1) and the zinc layer (Method 2). [1 mark]
fields.finalAnswer: (i) Barrier to air and moisture; (ii) zinc corrodes in preference to iron; (iii) stainless steel (alloy with Cr, Ni) resists rusting throughout — Method 3 is most effective long-term.

fields.questionText:
A student heats copper turnings in air and observes that they turn black. When hydrogen gas is then passed over the heated black substance, it turns reddish-brown again and water droplets are formed.

(i) Name the black substance formed and write its chemical formula. [1]
(ii) What type of reaction takes place when copper is heated in air? [1]
(iii) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of the black substance with hydrogen, and identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced. [2]
fields.answer: (i) Copper(II) oxide, CuO. (ii) Oxidation (combination of copper with oxygen): 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. (iii) CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (on heating); hydrogen is oxidised to water and copper(II) oxide is reduced to copper — a redox reaction.
solutionSteps: (i) The black substance is copper(II) oxide, CuO. [1 mark]
(ii) 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO; copper gains oxygen, so it is oxidation (a combination reaction). [1 mark]
(iii) CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (heat). [1 mark]
(iii) H₂ gains oxygen and is oxidised; CuO loses oxygen and is reduced to red-brown copper. [1 mark]
fields.finalAnswer: (i) CuO; (ii) oxidation (2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO); (iii) CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O — H₂ oxidised, CuO reduced.

fields.answer: Autotrophs are organisms that make their own food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, e.g. green plants. A school is organizing a grand cultural event to show the talent of its students. To accommodate the guests, the school plans to rent chairs and tables from a local supplier. It finds that the rent for each chair is ₹50 and for each table is ₹200. The school spends ₹30,000 for renting the chairs and tables. fields.answer: (i) x + y = 300 and 50x + 200y = 30000 (i.e. x + 4y = 600). (ii)(a) 200 chairs and 100 tables. OR (b) 220 chairs and 80 tables. (iii) 150 tables.

(iii) Number of tables = 30000 ÷ 200 = 150, so at most 150 tables can be rented if no chairs are rented. [1 mark]

fields.questionText: The sum of a two digit number and the number obtained by reversing the digits is 66. If the digits of the number differ by 2, find the number. How many such numbers are there?
fields.answer: The numbers are 42 and 24 (two such numbers).
solutionSteps: Let tens digit = x, units digit = y. Original number = 10x + y; reversed number = 10y + x. Sum: (10x + y) + (10y + x) = 66 ⇒ 11(x + y) = 66 ⇒ x + y = 6.
Digits differ by 2: either x − y = 2 or y − x = 2.
Case 1: x + y = 6 and x − y = 2 ⇒ x = 4, y = 2 → number = 42. Case 2: x + y = 6 and y − x = 2 ⇒ x = 2, y = 4 → number = 24. Two such numbers: 42 and 24.

fields.questionText:
The polynomial P(x) = x² − 3x − 4 models the profit (in lakh ₹, a negative value meaning a loss) of a small start-up x years after it opened.
(a) Factorise P(x) by splitting the middle term.
(b) Find the zeroes of P(x).
(c) Which zero gives a meaningful break-even time (profit zero)? Also verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients of P(x).
fields.answer: (a) P(x) = (x − 4)(x + 1). (b) Zeroes: 4 and −1. (c) Only x = 4 is meaningful (time cannot be negative), so break-even is after 4 years. Sum = 3 = −(−3)/1, product = −4 = −4/1 — verified.
fields.explanation: Split −3x as −4x + x: x² − 4x + x − 4 = x(x − 4) + 1(x − 4) = (x − 4)(x + 1). The zeroes are 4 and −1. Time x ≥ 0, so x = −1 is rejected and the start-up breaks even after 4 years. Sum of zeroes 3 = −b/a and product −4 = c/a.
solutionSteps: (c) Time cannot be negative, so x = −1 is rejected; break-even occurs at x = 4 years. [1]
fields.strategyHint: Split the middle term to factorise, then reject zeroes that make no sense in the real-world context.
fields.finalAnswer: (a) (x − 4)(x + 1). (b) 4 and −1. (c) x = 4 years is the only meaningful break-even time; sum 3 = −b/a, product −4 = c/a.

fields.questionText:
A school is organising a raffle draw in which 100 tickets are sold, numbered 1 to 100. Ramesh buys 2 of these tickets. One ticket is drawn at random for the first prize.
(i) What is the probability that the drawn ticket is one of Ramesh's tickets?
(ii) What is the probability that the drawn ticket is not one of Ramesh's tickets?
(iii) The school decides that the 5 tickets numbered 96 to 100 are reserved for teachers and removes them before the draw. Ramesh's tickets are not among them. Find the new probability that Ramesh wins the first prize, and the probability that he does not.
fields.answer: (i) 1/50 (ii) 49/50 (iii) P(wins) = 2/95, P(does not win) = 93/95
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Total outcomes = 100, favourable = 2, so P = 2/100 = 1/50
[1 mark] (ii) P(not Ramesh's) = 1 − 1/50 = 49/50
[1 mark] (iii) Tickets left in the draw = 100 − 5 = 95, of which Ramesh holds 2
[1 mark] (iii) P(Ramesh wins) = 2/95, so P(does not win) = 1 − 2/95 = 93/95

fields.questionText:
A carton has 24 bulbs, of which 6 are defective. One bulb is drawn at random.
(i) What is the probability that the bulb drawn is NOT defective? (1 mark)
(ii) Suppose the bulb drawn is defective and it is not put back. How many bulbs are now left in the carton, and how many of them are defective? (1 mark)
(iii) A second bulb is now drawn at random from the bulbs left in the carton (as in part (ii)). What is the probability that this second bulb is defective? (2 marks)
solutionSteps: (i) Non-defective bulbs = 24 − 6 = 18. P(not defective) = 18/24 = 3/4.
(ii) One defective bulb is removed: bulbs left = 24 − 1 = 23; defective bulbs left = 6 − 1 = 5.
(iii) Total possible outcomes for the second draw = 23 (all equally likely); favourable outcomes (defective) = 5.
(iii) P(second bulb defective) = 5/23.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) 3/4; (ii) 23 bulbs left, of which 5 are defective; (iii) 5/23

fields.questionText: Manu and Aiza are competing in a 60 km cycling race. Aiza's average speed is 10 km/hr greater than Manu's average speed and she finished the race in 1/2 hour less than Manu. Find the time taken by Manu to finish the race.
fields.answer: Manu took 2 hours.
solutionSteps: Let Manu's time = t hours, so Manu's speed = 60/t km/hr. Aiza's speed = 60/t + 10 and Aiza's time = t − 1/2.
Multiply by t: 10t^2 − 5t − 30 = 0 ⟹ 2t^2 − t − 6 = 0.
Factorise: (t − 2)(2t + 3) = 0 ⟹ t = 2 (reject t = −3/2).
Manu took 2 hours.

fields.question:
A ball is thrown upwards and its height h (in metres) after t seconds is given by h = −5t² + 20t.
(i) After how many seconds does the ball hit the ground?
(ii) At what times is the ball at a height of 15 m?
(iii) For what value of k will −5t² + 20t = k have equal roots? Hence find the greatest height reached by the ball and the time at which it is reached.
fields.answer: (i) t = 4 s. (ii) t = 1 s and t = 3 s. (iii) k = 20; greatest height 20 m, reached at t = 2 s.
fields.explanation: Each part is solved as a quadratic equation: h = 0 for landing, h = 15 for the given height, and equal roots (D = 0) for the single highest point.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) h = 0 ⟹ −5t² + 20t = 0 ⟹ 5t(4 − t) = 0 ⟹ t = 0 (launch) or t = 4. The ball hits the ground after 4 s.
[1 mark] (ii) −5t² + 20t = 15 ⟹ t² − 4t + 3 = 0 ⟹ (t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 ⟹ t = 1 s (going up) and t = 3 s (coming down).
[1 mark] (iii) 5t² − 20t + k = 0 has equal roots when D = (−20)² − 4(5)(k) = 400 − 20k = 0 ⟹ k = 20.
[1 mark] (iii) With k = 20 the ball reaches that height only once, so it is the greatest height, 20 m; the equal root t = 20/(2 × 5) = 2 s.
fields.finalAnswer: (i) 4 s; (ii) 1 s and 3 s; (iii) k = 20; greatest height 20 m at t = 2 s.

fields.questionText: Prove that √5 is an irrational number.
fields.answer: Assuming √5 = p/q (p, q co-prime integers, q ≠ 0) leads to 5 dividing both p and q, contradicting co-primality. Hence √5 is irrational.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Let √5 be rational: √5 = p/q, where p, q are co-prime integers and q ≠ 0. Squaring, 5q² = p², so 5 divides p², hence 5 divides p. Let p = 5a for some integer a.
[1 mark] Then 25a² = 5q² ⇒ q² = 5a², so 5 divides q², hence 5 divides q.
[1 mark] So 5 is a common factor of p and q, contradicting that p and q are co-prime. Hence √5 is irrational.

solutionSteps: Choose modal class 20-30 (so l = 20, h = 10) and target mode = 25.
